etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English singuler, from Old French, from Latin singulāris (“alone of its kind”), from Latin singulus (“single”).

definitions.definition: Being only one of a larger population; single, individual.

quote.citation: 1387–1400, Geoffrey Chaucer, “The Canon’s Yeoman’s Tale”, in The Canterbury Tales, [Westminster: William Caxton, published 1478], →OCLC;  Charles Cowden Clarke, editor, The Canterbury Tales of Chaucer. […], 2nd edition, volume III, Edinburgh: James Nichol; London: James Nisbet & Co.; Dublin: W. Robertson, 1860, →OCLC, page 158:
quote.text: And God forbid that all a company / Should rue a singular manne's folly.And may God forbid that a whole group should suffer for a single man's folly.

definitions.definition: Being the only one of the kind; unique.

quote.citation: 1705, J[oseph] Addison, Remarks on Several Parts of Italy, &c. in the Years 1701, 1702, 1703, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The busts […]  of the emperors and empresses are all very scarce, and some of them almost singular in their kind.

quote.citation: 1839, Charles Darwin, Narrative of the Surveying Voyages of His Majesty’s Ships Adventure and Beagle, between the Years 1826 and 1836, […], volume III, London: Henry Colburn, […], →OCLC, pages 461–462:
quote.text: A group of finches, of which Mr. Gould considers there are thirteen species; and these he has distributed into for new sub-genera. These birds are the most singular of any in the archipelago.

definitions.definition: Distinguished by superiority: peerless, unmatched, eminent, exceptional, extraordinary.

quote.citation: 1641 (first performance), [John Denham], The Sophy. […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for H[enry] Herringman, […], published 1667, →OCLC, Act I, scene ii, page 11:
quote.text: So ſingular a ſadneſs / Muſt have a cauſe as ſtrange as the effect:  […]

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book V”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: His zeal / None seconded, as out of season judged, / Or singular and rash.

definitions.definition: (grammar) Referring to only one thing or person.
(linear algebra, of matrix) Having no inverse.
(linear algebra, of transformation) Having the property that the matrix of coefficients of the new variables has a determinant equal to zero.
(set theory, of a cardinal number) Not equal to its own cofinality.
(obsolete) Engaged in by only one on a side; single.

quote.citation: 1577, Raphaell Holinshed, The Firste Volume of the Chronicles of England, Scotlande, and Irelande […], volume I, London:  […]  [Henry Bynneman] for Iohn Harrison, →OCLC:
quote.text: Thus made he an end, and the two princes allowed well of his last motion, and so order was taken, that they should fight togither in a singular combat

definitions.definition: (grammar) A form of a word that refers to only one person or thing.
(logic) That which is not general; a specific determinate instance.
